subject: Accounting
title: Return on Equity
description: Learn Return on Equity in one minute.

hook.text: You invest $100,000 in a business. It earns $15,000. Is that good? ROE tells you.

buildup.text: Return on equity divides net income by shareholders' equity.

discovery.text: A 15% ROE means the company generates $0.15 of profit for every dollar of equity.

twist.text: High ROE can be misleading if it's driven by massive debt rather than genuine efficiency.

climax.text: Buffett looks for consistently high ROE—it signals a durable competitive advantage.

punchline.text: ROE measures how hard your money works for you.

quiz.question: How is return on equity calculated?
options: Net income divided by shareholders' equity

details.summary: Return on equity measures how effectively a company uses shareholders' investment to generate profit. This topic explains ROE calculation, the DuPont decomposition that reveals its drivers, and how leverage can artificially inflate the metric.
details.whyItMatters: ROE tells shareholders how hard their capital is working. But high ROE from excessive leverage is risky, not impressive. Understanding ROE's components separates genuine efficiency from financial engineering.
takeaways: ROE equals net income divided by average shareholders' equity
DuPont analysis breaks ROE into profit margin × asset turnover × financial leverage
High ROE driven primarily by financial leverage (debt) carries more risk than ROE from margins or turnover

faq.question: How is return on equity calculated?
faq.answer: ROE equals net income divided by average shareholders' equity, expressed as a percentage. A 20% ROE means the company earned $0.20 for every dollar of equity invested. DuPont analysis breaks this into three components: profit margin, asset turnover, and leverage.

faq.question: Why can high ROE be misleading?
faq.answer: Adding debt reduces equity (the denominator), which mathematically increases ROE without improving actual profitability. DuPont decomposition separates leverage from operational efficiency. An ROE of 25% driven by excessive debt is far riskier than one driven by high margins.
